svg.aria-label: Diagnosing a blocked flow in Azure: effective security rules versus IP flow verify, how to read the output, the expanded service tag prefixes, and where both tools stop
svg.title: Diagnosing a blocked flow in Azure: what each of the two tools answers, how to read the aggregated rule output, the field that prints a service tag's real contents, and the limits of both
svg.text: The rule list says what was configured. Only the aggregation says what applies.
EFFECTIVE SECURITY RULES
“What rules are in force here?”
The aggregation of the group on the interface
and the group on the subnet it sits in.
Lives on the network interface
All protocols, as written
Network security groups only
Needs an attached group and a running VM
IP FLOW VERIFY
“Would THIS packet get through?”
Access allowed or Access denied, plus the name
of the one rule that decided, and a link to it.
Lives in Network Watcher
TCP and UDP only
Also covers Virtual Network Manager admin rules
No link given means a default rule decided
READING THE AGGREGATED OUTPUT
NetworkSecurityGroup — which group
Association — NetworkInterface or Subnet
defaultSecurityRules/ — one of the six defaults
securityRules/ — a rule you wrote
Duplicate rules are provenance, not error: a group linked to both the interface and the subnet
repeats its defaults and any shared custom rules.
The portal shows only the first 50 rules. Download the CSV for the real set.
THE FIELD THAT MAKES A SERVICE TAG CONCRETE
A rule naming Internet, VirtualNetwork or AzureLoadBalancer also carries
expandedDestinationAddressPrefix
— which lists every address prefix the tag represents, right now, for this interface.
For peered networks the VirtualNetwork tag expands to include the peers’ prefixes, visible in the
ExpandedAddressPrefix list.
So what the default inbound allow admits is measurable, not a matter of trust.
PRECONDITIONS AND LIMITS
· Effective rules return nothing without an attached group, and nothing if the VM is stopped —
two very different facts wearing the same clothes.
· No group and a public IP means every port open inbound and outbound, to and from anywhere.
· Rules differ per interface, so a two-NIC machine needs two queries. There is no subnet-wide answer.
· IP flow verify needs a Network Watcher instance in the VM’s own subscription and region.
· ICMP and scale sets go to NSG diagnostics instead.
WHEN BOTH TOOLS SAY ALLOWED AND IT STILL FAILS
The documented next causes are firewall software inside the guest operating system, and routes to
virtual appliances or on-premises.
Forced tunnelling of internet traffic can make a machine unreachable from the internet while every
rule reads correctly. That is the point to stop diagnosing filtering and start on routing.
THE TEST THAT PASSES WHILE PRODUCTION FAILS
Windows RPC connects to port 135, then to a dynamic port in 49152-65535. A 135-only test succeeds
while the real connection is blocked. Verify the host’s range rather than assuming the default.
